title: Chanting for the dying
hookLine: a sick elder in a cave, and the Buddha reciting what the sick man already knew
tomorrow: who looks after the one doing all the looking after?

lines: A CAVE, AN ELDER IN PAIN.
cards: In some hospital rooms there's a phone on the windowsill playing the songs a grandmother used to sing while she cooked. She hasn't spoken in days. Nobody is sure she can hear.
They play them anyway. So why chant to someone too sick to answer? Here's a scene from the suttas.
Evening. A cave in the hills. Maha Kassapa, one of the Buddha's great elders, lies there sick and in pain.
The Buddha comes out of his seclusion, sits down beside him, and asks: are you bearing up? And Kassapa tells the truth. No.

teach.b: The Buddha doesn't bring medicine. He begins to recite. He names the seven factors of awakening, one by one: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Each, he says, when developed, leads to awakening. None of this is news to Kassapa.
He has practiced these for years. That's the point. The Buddha isn't teaching him something new.
He's reminding a tired mind of what it already knows, in a voice it trusts. It's like a parent reading a bedtime story the child knows by heart. The child isn't learning the plot.
The child is being held by it.
The sutta says Kassapa delighted in the words, and he rose from that illness. His answer had been no. After the recitation, it changed.
Buddhists took the lesson to heart.
These verses became a protective chant, a paritta, sung for the sick to this day. Other schools have their own bedside sounds. In Pure Land homes it's the name of Amida Buddha.
In Tibetan homes, prayers read aloud near the dying. The tradition doesn't promise every sick person will rise like Kassapa.
What it holds is this: a chant at the bedside steadies the one who hears it, and it steadies the ones singing it too. Even when no one can answer.

how: Theravada monks and lay people chant protective verses (paritta), including the factors of awakening, for the sick and dying; Pure Land Buddhists say the nembutsu at the bedside, and Tibetan Buddhists read prayers and texts aloud near the dying.

games.q: what does “chanting for the dying” mean?
o: singing loudly to keep evil spirits out of a sickroom
a ceremony that decides where a person is reborn
sounding familiar teachings aloud to steady someone near death

games.q: in the cave — tap the pairs.
p: a great elder, sick and in pain
a protective chant for the sick

s: chanting at a bedside only works if the sick person understands Pali
in the sutta Kassapa knew the teaching already; the chant reminded him. and it steadies the ones who sing it too.
in the sutta, the Buddha recited teachings Kassapa already knew
the seven factors of awakening, which Kassapa had long practiced.
the tradition promises that chanting will cure anyone who hears it
Kassapa rose from that illness, but the tradition doesn't promise every sick person will.

games.q: your friend's grandfather loved one old song. he's in hospice now and doesn't respond. his family wonders whether to play it. what fits the story in the cave?
o: skip it; if he can't respond, he can't hear, so it does nothing.
play it softly; something he knows by heart can reach him and steady the room.
play something new and calming instead, so it doesn't stir up memories.
games.why: the Buddha recited what Kassapa already knew, in a voice he trusted. a familiar sound reminds; and it holds the people singing too.

practice: Say the seven factors slowly out loud, in Pali, one per breath, letting each word take its time: sati, dhammavicaya, viriya, piti, passaddhi, samadhi, upekkha. Then go through them again, a little softer.
If the Pali feels too strange, say the English instead: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity.

wordCard.voice: Chanting for the dying: reciting what a tired mind already knows, so the one who hears it, and the ones who sing, are steadied.

orig.note: Pali bojjhanga: a factor of awakening; the seven are recited for the sick.

carryVoice: Your line: a chant at the bedside, a reminder in a voice someone trusts. Day twenty-one of thirty, sung.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 46.14, Gilana Sutta (Maha Kassapa sick; the Buddha recites the seven factors of awakening; Kassapa delights and recovers)
